advisory.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm the regression test's `corrupt_ref_lock.read_pause.call_count == 0` assertion meaningfully distinguishes the read_pause stub's effect (it is trivially true since all _load_ref_lock callers are stubbed).
evidence: Regression test patches `_load_ref_lock` to return corrupt_ref_lock: `patch(f"{_ADVISORY_LOCK_KEY}._load_ref_lock", return_value=corrupt_ref_lock)`

But `_stub_main_advisory` first stubs read_pause: `stack.enter_context(patch(f"{_ADVISORY_LOCK_KEY}.read_pause", read_pause_mock))` plus check_pass_lock/check_phase_gate/acquire_pass_lock/release_pass_lock
_advisory_lock.py:128,145,181,200,210,227,234 — every `_load_ref_lock()` call site is inside one of the five functions that the helper stubs, so a fully-stubbed main() never invokes _load_ref_lock

ABSENCE: the assertion `corrupt_ref_lock.read_pause.call_count == 0` cannot fail given the stub set, so it does not verify the specific guard the docstring claims ('the guard is not bought by going blind' rests on the manual RED run, not the test as written)
advisory.finding: In the regression test, the `_load_ref_lock` patch that produces `corrupt_ref_lock` is never exercised because `_stub_main_advisory` stubs all five advisory entry points (read_pause, check_pass_lock, check_phase_gate, acquire_pass_lock, release_pass_lock) at the `_advisory_lock` module level, and those are the only callers of `_load_ref_lock`. The `corrupt_ref_lock.read_pause.call_count == 0` assertion is therefore trivially satisfied and does not actually prove the read_pause stub (vs. any other stub) is what prevents reaching the corrupt layer.
